passage:
Friday, 8 pm.
Today at lunch I grabbed Nirmala's new gel pen and wouldn't give it back. When she reached for it I pulled so hard it snapped in two. She went quiet and her eyes got shiny. I said, "It was already broken," which was a lie. My stomach hurt all afternoon.
After school I walked to her gate. I said, "I'm sorry I broke your pen, and I lied. I did it because I was showing off." She didn't say anything for a bit. Then she said, "Okay." I gave her two pens from my own pencil box and helped her stick her diary cover back, which had ripped too.
We played catch after that. Mummy asked why I looked lighter. I don't know.
— Ritu

qa.q: What did Ritu give Nirmala after breaking the pen?
qa.a: Ritu gave Nirmala two pens from Ritu's own pencil box.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling during the afternoon after breaking the pen?
qa.a: Ritu felt guilty and uneasy, shown by the stomach ache all afternoon and the lie about the pen already being broken.

qa.q: What made it possible for Ritu to play catch afterwards?
qa.a: Ritu said sorry, admitted the lie and the showing off, and helped repair things by giving pens and fixing the diary cover. The repair came before the lighter feeling.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt when Ritu turned up at her gate?
qa.a: Nirmala was probably still hurt and unsure, since she said nothing for a bit and then only "Okay." Ritu's honest apology and the offered pens may have helped her feel respected.

grounding: A child who hurt a friend apologises and helps fix things, then is able to play again.

passage:
On the threshing floor after harvest, Kiran's kite would not rise while Omkar's soared over the neem tree. Kiran's face went hot. When Omkar left his kite on the ground and went to drink water, Kiran stamped on it. The bamboo frame cracked in the middle.
Omkar came back, said nothing, and walked home carrying the pieces. Kiran's ears burned all the way to supper.
The next morning Kiran knocked on Omkar's door. "I broke your kite on purpose. I was jealous. I'm sorry. Can I fix it?"
Omkar looked at him for a long moment. "Bring flour paste."
They spent the afternoon splitting new bamboo and pasting paper. By evening the kite flew, wobbling, over the fields, and both boys ran after it, laughing.

qa.q: What did Kiran stamp on?
qa.a: Kiran stamped on Omkar's kite.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling after breaking the kite?
qa.a: Kiran felt ashamed and guilty, with burning ears all the way to supper.

qa.q: What did Kiran do that let the two boys play together again?
qa.a: Kiran went to Omkar's door, admitted breaking it on purpose out of jealousy, apologised and offered to fix it, then did the work.

qa.q: What might Omkar have been feeling when he walked home carrying the pieces without a word?
qa.a: Omkar was probably hurt and angry, and perhaps sad about the kite. Saying nothing suggests he did not trust himself to speak.

grounding: A child who hurt a friend apologises and helps mend the damage, then is able to play again.

passage: In the courtyard of their apartment block in Addis Ababa, Abebe got angry when Mina's kite flew higher than his. He grabbed her string and yanked, and the kite tore on the railing. Mina burst into tears and ran inside. Abebe stood alone with his own kite, feeling sick. He didn't want to fly it anymore. After ten minutes he knocked on Mina's door. "I'm sorry I pulled it. I was jealous." Mina sniffed. "It's ripped." "My grandmother has tape and paper. Can I help fix it?" They sat on the stairs with his grandmother's tape, patching the torn corner with an old calendar page. It looked funny, but it held. By evening both kites were up again. Abebe laughed out loud when Mina's patched one wobbled past his, and the sick feeling was gone.

qa.q: What did Abebe and Mina use to patch the kite?
qa.a: They used his grandmother's tape and an old calendar page.

qa.q: How did Abebe feel standing alone after the kite tore?
qa.a: He felt sick and guilty, so bad that he didn't want to fly his own kite anymore.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Apologising honestly and helping repair the kite worked, because it fixed the harm and let both children play together again.

qa.q: How might Mina have felt when Abebe offered to help?
qa.a: Mina was probably still hurt, but comforted that he admitted his jealousy and wanted to make it right.

grounding: Shows a child who hurt a friend apologising and helping repair the damage, after which he can play again and the guilt eases.

passage: During the Class 4 art period at Greenfield School, Chaitanya bumped Elizabeth's water jar on purpose because she had laughed at his drawing. Grey water ran all over her painted lighthouse. Elizabeth stared at it, then put her head down on the desk. Chaitanya felt his face burn. He spent the next five minutes pretending to sharpen a pencil. Then he went over. "I did that on purpose. I'm sorry. I was cross because you laughed." Elizabeth lifted her head. "It's ruined." "Can I help you paint a new one? I'm good at waves." Their teacher gave them a fresh sheet. Chaitanya did the waves, Elizabeth did the lighthouse. At break, they played tag together as if nothing had happened, and Chaitanya ran faster than he had all week.

qa.q: What had Elizabeth painted?
qa.a: A lighthouse.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling while he pretended to sharpen a pencil?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and guilty, his face burning, unsure how to face Elizabeth.

qa.q: Why did helping paint the new picture matter more than just saying sorry?
qa.a: It actually repaired the damage and let them do something together, so both could move past it and play at break.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt when Chaitanya admitted it was on purpose?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and a little relieved that he told the truth, which made it easier to trust his offer of help.

grounding: Shows a child who spoiled a classmate's work apologising and helping repair it, then being able to play freely again.

passage: I'm Zubin's neighbour on the fourth floor, and I saw the whole thing from our balcony. Zubin and Manjula were building a fort from old cartons on the terrace. They argued about the door, and Zubin kicked the whole side in. Manjula shouted and sat down with her back to him. Zubin stood there for a long time, kicking at nothing. I don't know what he was thinking. Then he went downstairs and came back with more cartons and a roll of tape from his mother. He said something to Manjula that I couldn't hear. She shrugged. He started rebuilding the side by himself. After a while, she began holding the cartons for him. By sunset the fort had a new door, a bigger one. I heard them both laughing inside it.

qa.q: Where were Zubin and Manjula building the fort?
qa.a: On the terrace, from old cartons.

qa.q: What does Zubin standing there kicking at nothing suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt upset and uneasy, perhaps guilty, though the neighbour can't be sure what he was thinking.

qa.q: What small step did Zubin take to repair things?
qa.a: He fetched more cartons and tape, said something to Manjula, and started rebuilding the side he broke by himself.

qa.q: How did Manjula's feelings seem to change?
qa.a: She went from shouting and turning her back to holding the cartons and laughing inside the fort, which suggests she felt ready to forgive.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a child repair the fort he broke, after which both children could play again.

passage:
Tuesday. In the art period, Maria yanked the blue crayon out of Arohi's hand so hard that Arohi's drawing of her grandmother's house tore right through the roof. Arohi cried. Maria said, "It was already torn," and went back to her own page, but she couldn't colour anything properly all afternoon.
Wednesday. Maria waited by Arohi's bench before assembly. "I tore it. I'm sorry. I was mean about the crayon." She held out a roll of clear tape and a fresh sheet. They taped the roof from the back, and Maria redrew the chimney, very carefully.
Friday. At break Arohi called, "Maria, you're on my team!" and Maria ran over, lighter than she had felt all week.

qa.q: What did Maria bring to Arohi on Wednesday?
qa.a: She brought a roll of clear tape and a fresh sheet.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling on Tuesday afternoon after making her excuse?
qa.a: She felt guilty and uneasy, which is why she couldn't colour anything properly even though she had said it was already torn.

qa.q: Which choice helped Maria feel better, and why?
qa.a: Owning the tear and helping fix the drawing, because real repair eased her guilt in a way the excuse never did.

qa.q: How might Arohi have felt when Maria redrew the chimney?
qa.a: She probably felt cared for and ready to forgive, which is why she picked Maria for her team on Friday.

grounding: Shows a child who hurt a friend apologising and helping repair the harm, and then feeling free to play again.
